rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs while limiting the time penalty. The retention pattern will guide trimming the solvent window and testing slope or temperature selectivity.

Halve the gradient slope while keeping temperature and endpoints fixed to test whether the clustered peaks separate through slope selectivity. The short scouting retention times leave room for this diagnostic without a large time penalty.
The shallower gradient resolved most of the cluster but left one nearly co-eluting pair. Raise temperature while holding the gradient fixed to test selectivity for that pair and shorten retention.

Keep the favorable high-temperature selectivity and make the gradient one step shallower to improve the remaining R = 1.10 pair. The last peak at 8.56 minutes leaves room to gain resolution while staying below the time-penalty threshold.

The remaining close pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so reverse direction and steepen to 18 minutes. This should improve that pair and shorten the run, while testing whether the earlier R = 1.61 pair retains sufficient resolution.

The best method is only slightly short of full resolution, with R = 1.46 for one pair. Lower temperature by one step while preserving the gradient to seek a small selectivity improvement without incurring a time penalty.

Return to 60 C and raise the starting organic fraction while preserving the best run’s gradient slope. This tests a small solvent-window selectivity shift to lift the R = 1.46 pair above threshold while shortening retention.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 7 to improve its two early close pairs while preserving the later pair’s resolution margin. The narrowed endpoint remains comfortably above the observed elution window, targeting full resolution below 10 minutes.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.04583 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to lift the R = 1.49 pair above threshold. The later critical pair has some margin at R = 1.64, and the last peak should remain inside the gradient and below 10 minutes.

Injection 9 reached the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Raise the starting organic fraction and narrow the window to seek a shorter fully resolved separation, using the shallower slope to offset early-peak compression.

Keep the shorter-retention starting composition and reduce the slope to recover the early R = 1.08 pair. This tests whether full resolution can be restored before the later R = 1.78 pair loses its margin; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

The 60 C neighborhood shows opposing resolution constraints, so test a substantially different temperature for another selectivity regime. Keep injection 9’s gradient fixed to isolate temperature effects while retaining that maximum-score method as the benchmark.

The 25 C run nearly resolved every pair, revealing a promising alternative selectivity regime. Increase temperature one step with the gradient unchanged to test improvement of the R = 1.18 pair while shortening retention.

Test a narrower, higher-starting window in the low-temperature selectivity regime to shorten retention while using a shallower slope to improve the close central pair. Injection 9 remains the proven maximum-score method.

Continue narrowing the low-temperature gradient window by raising phi0 one step. The previous change improved the sole critical pair and shortened retention, so this tests whether that trend reaches full resolution.

Combine a modest temperature increase with a shallower gradient to improve the central close pair at the higher starting composition. The other pairs have useful resolution margins, and the previous 8.10-minute last peak leaves room for this adjustment.

Test an intermediate-temperature selectivity regime with a compact gradient window, seeking a faster fully resolved alternative. Injection 9 already secures the maximum CRF, so this run explores temperature-driven separation of the remaining close-pair patterns.

Steepen the 45 C gradient by one endpoint step to test whether both close pairs move away from their selectivity crossings. This also shortens retention, offering a potential faster alternative to injection 9.

The remaining close pair barely responds to slope, so lower temperature one step to change selectivity while retaining the faster gradient. Monitor the neighboring pair for a crossing; injection 9 remains the proven maximum-score method.

Test a steeper gradient at 35 C to seek a faster separation in a different elution-order regime. Injection 9 already attains the maximum possible CRF and remains the fallback if these selectivity changes introduce close pairs.

Refine injection 14 with a slightly shallower slope to lift its sole R = 1.40 pair above threshold. Its 8.75-minute last peak leaves room for this adjustment without a time penalty, potentially providing another maximum-score method.

Lengthen injection 15’s gradient one step to recover its central close pair while retaining the higher starting organic fraction. This tests a narrower-window alternative to the fully resolved injection 21; injection 9 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Test a higher starting composition with a shallower, narrower gradient to shorten the fully resolved low-temperature separation while preserving its central-pair resolution. Injection 9 remains the fastest proven method with the maximum CRF.

Probe a slope between injections 7 and 8 to bracket the faster side of the high-temperature resolution limit. Injection 9 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method and already achieves the maximum possible CRF.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 9 to improve its early critical pairs while checking whether the later pair retains full resolution. Injection 9 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method; this final run probes the opposite edge of its resolution window.
